query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short, controlled sub‐glass-transition isothermal anneal immediately following rapid quenching improves both the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous phosphorus-containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloy by relaxing free volume and promoting a more homogeneous short‐range order.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex metallic alloys in their metastable amorphous (glassy) state produced by rapid quenching.
generation.intervention: Apply a brief, sub‐Tg isothermal anneal immediately after rapid quenching, with annealing temperature set slightly below the glass transition temperature and hold time carefully controlled to avoid crystallization.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied immediately post-quench under controlled sub-Tg thermal conditions; it should benefit alloys where free volume relaxation without triggering crystallization is feasible. It may not work if the annealing temperature/time is too high/long, or for compositions with particularly low Tg margins.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction of internal free volume and a more uniform short-range atomic arrangement.
generation.mechanism: The sub-Tg anneal allows atomic rearrangements that relieve internal stresses and homogenize local chemical order without supplying enough energy for nucleation and growth of crystalline phases, thereby increasing both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-quenched baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit a higher resistance to crystallization upon subsequent heating (indicated by delayed onset of crystallization in DSC) and an enhanced overall stability of the amorphous state.
generation.baseline: The same alloy produced by rapid quenching without any post-quench thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be effective only within a narrow window of sub-Tg temperatures and hold times; outside this window, either insufficient free volume relaxation or premature crystallization may occur.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal sub-Tg annealing temperature and time may vary with alloy composition and cooling conditions; more work is needed to quantify the adjustment range and ensure that the intervention does not inadvertently trigger crystallization in some phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys via rapid quenching. Subject the experimental set to a controlled sub-Tg isothermal anneal (with systematically varied temperatures and hold times within the sub-Tg regime) and leave the control set as-quenched. Heat both sets under identical controlled conditions (using differential scanning calorimetry and in situ XRD) to monitor crystallization onset and overall thermal stability. Compare the crystallization temperatures, exothermic peak intensities, and microstructural features post-heating.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to record Tg and crystallization onset temperatures
In situ or post-process X-ray diffraction (XRD) or transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess amorphous versus crystalline phases
Measurement of free volume and short-range order via positron annihilation spectroscopy or other applicable techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sub-Tg annealed alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature or improved homogeneity in the amorphous structure compared to the as-quenched controls, or if they display early crystallization during the sub-Tg anneal, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

decision.trend: Early work in compositionally complex alloys has largely focused on tuning crystallization and phase‐decomposition phenomena either by adjusting alloy compositions (often using multi‐parameter modifications) or by varying the thermal processing protocols. For example, in PMC6197204 the study examined how annealing temperature drove phase separation in high‐entropy alloys, while in PMC12298864 mechanical alloying combined with spark plasma sintering was used to refine microstructures, where the evolution of nanocrystalline phases was sensitive to processing conditions. These studies demonstrate that even in complex alloys, controlling the thermal history (annealing temperature/time) is a powerful lever to influence metastability and suppress undesired transformations. However, previous attempts could not isolate a single, well‐defined intervention that simultaneously enhances both glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of an amorphous state in phosphorus‐containing versions of these alloys.
decision.unsolved: The key unsolved issue is how to identify and implement a single intervention that improves the ability to form a stable amorphous (glassy) state while retarding crystallization during subsequent thermal processing. In phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, the competition between rapid quenching to obtain the metastable glass and the inherent propensity for crystallization on heating remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Implement a short, controlled sub‐glass-transition isothermal anneal (sub‐Tg annealing) immediately after rapid quenching
decision.why: This approach is a natural extension of the trend toward using refined thermal processing to tailor metastable states observed in earlier studies. A brief anneal at a temperature below Tg can relax free volume and promote a more homogenous short-range order without triggering crystallization, thus improving both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous phase. This single thermal treatment lever is specific and testable via systematic variation of sub‐Tg temperature and hold time, and its effectiveness can be benchmarked against an otherwise comparable baseline alloy.
